title: How to use StayOnMap — and how not to
seoTitle: How to Use the App: What's Allowed, What's Not
description: How to search, contact an owner, book a visit and write a review that helps someone — plus what gets an account banned, and why nobody rates tenants here.
excerpt: The whole app in one read: how to search, how to contact an owner, how reviews actually work, and the short list of things that will get an account closed.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters and owners who built the thing

hero.alt: A phone showing a map of a city with rental price pins scattered across neighbourhoods

faq.q: Does StayOnMap charge tenants a brokerage fee?
faq.a: No. Tenants pay nothing — not to search, not to contact an owner, not to move in. If anyone on this platform asks you for a fee, a commission, or a payment in exchange for access to a listing, that is the single fastest way to get an account permanently closed. Report it and stop replying.

faq.q: Can a landlord rate me as a tenant?
faq.a: No, and this is deliberate. There is no tenant rating on StayOnMap and no plan to add one. Reviews here are of homes and neighbourhoods, never of people. A rating attached to a person becomes a quiet blacklist, and in Indian rentals that blacklist would fill up with exactly the things people are already refused housing over.

Usually yes. Most reviews publish the moment you submit them. A review goes to a human first if it is strongly negative, or if our integrity checks see something worth a second look — a brand-new account, every category scored identically, or one account reviewing the same landlord repeatedly.

faq.q: Does the owner find out that I reported their listing?
faq.a: The owner is shown what was reported and can respond to it. They are never shown who filed it. That holds whether or not you tick the anonymous box — your identity is stripped server-side before an owner sees anything, because a safety feature that reveals the reporter is a retaliation feature.

faq.q: Why can I only see some owners' phone numbers?
faq.a: Because a number appears only if that person chose to share it. Someone who has not shared one and someone who never saved one look identical on purpose — you see no call button either way, with no explanation. Use the in-app chat instead; it is the record that protects both sides if a disagreement turns into a dispute.

body:
Most rental platforms in India are a list of listings with a map bolted on the side. StayOnMap is the other way round: the map *is* the product, and everything else floats on top of it. That one decision changes how you use the app, so it is worth ten minutes to learn properly — and it is worth knowing the handful of things that will get an account closed, because that list is shorter and stricter than you might expect.

This is the practical guide. The formal version, split by whether you are an owner, a tenant or a property manager, lives on the [Community Rules](/rules) page, and that page is the one that actually governs an account.

## Start with the map, not a search box

Open the app and you are looking at a map with prices on it. There is no "enter a city" step, because the honest first question in a house hunt is not *which city* — you already know that — it is *which part of it can I afford, and how far is it from the thing I do every day*.

So: pan and zoom to the area you actually care about. The count near the top tells you how many homes are in the view you are looking at, and it updates as you move. Tap it to see those same homes as a list. The list and the map always agree, because they are the same query.

A few things worth knowing:

- **Six categories, not one.** Flats, houses, land, PG beds, shops and short stays are all here, and the app changes shape for each. A plot does not get asked how many bedrooms it has, and a shop is measured against footfall rather than schools.
- **Rent or lease.** In much of south India the deal is a refundable lump sum rather than a monthly rent. The toggle in the filters switches between them, and prices are labelled so you never mistake an eight-lakh lease for eight lakhs a month.
- **Around forty filters.** Deposit, furnishing, floor, pets, bachelors, gated, power backup, distance to a metro. Use two or three, not twenty — over-filtering an inventory this size hides homes you would have liked.
- **The heart saves it.** Saved homes get their own tab, and the recommendations you see are built from what you saved rather than from anything you typed.

If you want the argument for why a map beats a list at all, it is [here](/blog/why-maps-beat-lists-for-finding-a-home).

## Contacting an owner, and what happens next

Tap a pin and you get the real listing: photos, the price broken down into rent, deposit and maintenance, what is nearby, and what the area is actually like. From there you have three moves.

**Message the owner.** Chat is in the app, and it stays in the app. This is the part people are tempted to skip — someone sends a WhatsApp number, you move the conversation there, and now the only record of what was promised is on a phone that either of you can delete. Keep it here. If a disagreement becomes a dispute later, the thread is the evidence, and our support team can read it.

**Call, if there is a number.** Some people share a phone number and some do not. You will see a call button only if they did.

**Book a visit.** Pick a date and a time and send the request. The owner accepts, rejects, or proposes another slot, and you both get told. Then — and this matters more than it sounds — *show up*. An owner blocking out a Saturday morning for a viewing that nobody attends is the most common complaint we get from the listing side, and "they never turned up" is the reason a lot of good owners stop replying quickly to anyone.

If you agree to take the place, the owner sends a lease offer through the app: dates, rent, deposit. You sign it or you reject it. Nothing about that step costs you anything.

Which brings up the thing worth repeating: **tenants pay StayOnMap nothing, ever.** No brokerage, no listing fee, no "unlock the contact details" charge. The entire reason this platform exists is that a month or two of rent disappearing to somebody who unlocked a door is a bad deal. Anyone asking you for money to see a flat is misusing the platform, and there is a report button for exactly that.

## How reviews actually work

After you have lived somewhere — or seriously tried to — you can review it. A review here is not a star and a sentence. It is **twelve separate ratings**: safety, cleanliness, water, noise, internet, parking, the neighbourhood, transport, maintenance, how the owner behaved, security, and power backup. Then a written bit.

Twelve categories is more work than one, and that is on purpose. "3 stars" tells the next person nothing. "Water is a 2, everything else is a 4" tells them exactly what they are signing up for, and water in an Indian city is the sort of thing you find out in June when it is too late.

**Most reviews publish immediately.** We used to send every single one to a moderator, which meant honest reviews — the overwhelming majority — sat in a queue behind nothing while the genuinely urgent ones got buried. Now a review goes live as you submit it, and a human reads it first only in two cases:

- it is strongly negative, because a complaint is the one that can be a smear, a rival, or a grudge — and it is also the one the next renter most needs to be accurate;
- or something about *how* it was written looks off.

On that second point, we would rather be open than clever. We look at whether the twelve categories all got the same score, whether the review was submitted faster than the form can physically be read, whether the account was created minutes beforehand, and whether one account keeps reviewing listings belonging to the same landlord. None of those prove anything on their own — a genuinely delighted tenant really does give twelve fives — so none of them reject a review. They just mean a person reads it before it goes up.

If you own the listing, you can reply to any review, publicly, and your reply sits underneath it. That is usually a better answer than disputing it. "The tank was being replaced that month, it is fixed now" reads as an owner who is paying attention. Silence reads as agreement.

Writing a good review earns points. Points are private, are shown to nobody else, are not a leaderboard, and cannot be exchanged for anything — they exist to say thank you for helping the next person, not to make you open the app daily.

## You rate homes here. Not people.

This is the question we get most from owners, so here is the plain answer: **there is no way to rate a tenant on StayOnMap, and we are not going to build one.**

It is not an oversight and it is not on a roadmap. A rating attached to a person is a blacklist with a friendlier name, and anyone who has looked for a flat in an Indian city knows precisely what would end up in it — being single, being a bachelor, eating meat, the wrong surname, the wrong religion, a woman living alone. Housing discrimination here does not need a scoring system to help it along.

What an owner *does* get is real, and it is enough:

- **A verified badge**, by proving you own the place. That is the trust signal that belongs on a rental platform — evidence about the property, not gossip about a person.
- **A public reply** to any review or report on your listing.
- **A report button** for a specific person who has actually done something — abuse in chat, a no-show pattern, harassment. That goes to our support team with the conversation attached, and it is judged case by case by a human.
- **Block**, which ends the conversation immediately.

An owner's own standing is *computed*, not voted on. It comes from whether the listing is verified, how fast messages get answered, and what the reviews of the property say. You cannot be marked down by someone who never rented from you.

## What gets an account banned

The full list is on [Community Rules](/rules), split by role. These are the ones that end an account rather than earn a warning.

| Behaviour | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Demanding commission or cash to show a listing | Permanent ban. No warnings, no appeal. |
| Listing a property you do not own or manage | Listing removed, account reviewed |
| Fake or placeholder listings, or the same home posted repeatedly | Detected automatically, raises your risk score, listing suspended |
| Bait-and-switch on price after a visit | Listing suspended |
| Discriminating on religion, caste, gender or marital status | Account reviewed, and we do act on it |
| Posting fake reviews, for or against a property | Review removed, account reviewed |
| Asking anyone for identity documents or bank details | Account reviewed |
| Harassment or abuse in chat | Account reviewed, blocking available immediately |

Two notes on that table. The first row genuinely has no appeal — removing the practice of handing over months of rent to an intermediary is the reason this platform was built, so it is the one rule with no second chance. And the third row is not a human noticing: duplicate addresses, near-identical coordinates, photos already uploaded by someone else, and one phone number behind several "owner" accounts are all detected automatically.

A blocked account cannot do anything — not browse as a signed-in user, not message, not list. It is not a partial restriction.

> StayOnMap will never ask you for your Aadhaar, your PAN, a bank account number, or an OTP. Not by email, not in chat, not on a call. Anyone who does is not us.

## If something goes wrong

Report the listing from the listing itself. You can do it anonymously, and it works whether or not you are signed in. The owner is shown what was said and can respond; the owner is **never** shown who said it, ticked box or not. That is enforced on the server, not in the app, because a report that identifies the reporter is not a safety feature.

For anything else — a dispute, a stuck deposit, a listing that will not go live, an account you cannot get into — open a support case from the menu. A case has a history, can be replied to and reopened, and gets assigned to an actual person. That is a better route than emailing, because the thread stays attached to the listing or the conversation it is about.

If you are new to renting in India generally, rather than to this app, start with [the questions worth asking before you rent](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) and [how rental scams actually work](/blog/rental-scams-in-india). The second one is dull reading right up until the week it saves you a deposit.
